sections.title: Nominative
sections.html:
The case of the subject: the one who does the action, or the thing a sentence is about. A word describing the subject (an adjective or participle) is also nominative.

In our texts: cittaṃ … saṃvattati, “the mind … leads”; dhammā uppajjanti, “qualities arise”.

sections.title: Accusative
sections.html:
The case of the direct object, and of the goal of a verb of motion. The neuter accusative singular is also used as an adverb.

In our texts: buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, “I go to the Buddha as refuge”; dutiyaṃ, “for the second time”.

sections.title: Instrumental
sections.html:
“By, with, by means of”. It also expresses cause: “because of, on account of”.

In our texts: yena … nūppajjanti, “on account of which … do not arise”.

sections.title: Dative
sections.html:
“To, for”. Very common for purpose or result, especially with saṃvattati, “leads to”, and with abstract nouns: “for the sake of …”. It also marks the person for whom something is so.

In our texts: mahato anatthāya saṃvattati, “leads to great harm”; pahānāya, “for the abandoning”; micchādiṭṭhikassa, “for one of wrong view”.

sections.html:

sections.title: Genitive
sections.html:
“Of”: possession and other relations between two nouns. Its forms are often the same as the dative’s, so the context decides.

In our texts: anuppannānaṃ … dhammānaṃ anuppādāya, “for the non-arising of unarisen … qualities”.

sections.title: Vocative
sections.html:
The case of address: the person or people spoken to.

In our texts: bhikkhave, “O bhikkhus” (vocative plural of bhikkhu).

sections.title: Present tense
sections.html:
Describes what happens now, what usually happens, or a general truth. The endings show person and number.

singularplural
3rd persongacchatigacchanti
2nd persongacchasigacchatha
1st persongacchāmigacchāma

In our texts: saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, “I go for refuge”; samanupassāmi, “I see”; saṃvattati, “it leads”; uppajjanti, “they arise”.

sections.title: Imperative
sections.html:
Commands, requests and wishes: “go!”, “may he go”.

singularplural
3rd persongacchatugacchantu
2nd persongaccha, gacchāhigacchatha
1st persongacchāmigacchāma

sections.title: Optative
sections.html:
What should, would or might happen: advice, possibility and conditions. Recognise it by -eyya- (and the short 3rd person singular in -e).

singularplural
3rd persongaccheyya, gacchegaccheyyuṃ
2nd persongaccheyyāsigaccheyyātha
1st persongaccheyyāmigaccheyyāma

sections.title: Future tense
sections.html: What will happen. Recognise it by -issa-: gacchissati, “he will go”; gacchissanti, “they will go”.

sections.title: Aorist (past tense)
sections.html: The usual past tense of narrative: “he went, they said”. Many verbs form it with -i (3rd singular) and -iṃsu (3rd plural): pucchi, “he asked”; pucchiṃsu, “they asked”. Several common verbs are irregular.

sections.title: Past participle
sections.html:
A verbal adjective in -ta or -na: “tamed, arisen, guarded”. Like any adjective it agrees with its noun in gender, case and number, and it can also stand as the main verb of a sentence.

In our texts: dantaṃ cittaṃ, “a tamed mind”; uppannā dhammā, “arisen qualities”. With the prefix a(n)-: adanta, anuppanna.

sections.title: Present participle
sections.html: A verbal adjective in -nta or -māna: “going, seeing”. It describes an action happening at the same time as the main verb.

sections.title: Absolutive
sections.html: An indeclinable verb form in -tvā, -ya or -tvāna: “having done”. It describes an action completed before the main verb, by the same subject.

sections.title: Infinitive
sections.html: “To do”: an indeclinable form in -tuṃ, often expressing purpose: gantuṃ, “to go”.

sections.title: Sandhi and compounds
sections.html:
When two words meet, their sounds often join and change (sandhi). In our texts:

  • The parts of a compound are separated by a hyphen: dhammavādī → dhamma-vādī.
  • Where sandhi changes the sounds, an apostrophe goes with the first word: dhamma + anupassī → dhamm’ānupassī (not dhammā’nupassī).
  • But when the change reflects the grammar of the first word and not the second, the apostrophe goes before the second word: dhammo + amhi → dhammo’mhi (not dhamm’omhi).

sections.title: Pronouns
sections.html:
Personal pronouns (ahaṃ, “I”) and the relative pronoun ya-, “who, which”, which opens a clause of its own. The relative clause is often picked up by a word in the main clause.

In our texts: aññaṃ ekadhammaṃ … yaṃ evaṃ … saṃvattati, “one other thing which thus leads …”; yena, “on account of which”.

sections.title: Indeclinables
sections.html: Words that never change their form: particles, conjunctions and adverbs such as ca “and”, vā “or”, pi “also, even”, evaṃ “thus”, na “not” and iti, which closes a quotation.

sections.title: Adjectives
sections.html:
An adjective takes the gender, case and number of the noun it describes, and may stand before or after it.

In our texts: kusalā dhammā (masculine nominative plural); mahato anatthāya (masculine dative singular).

sections.title: Numbers
sections.html: Ordinals such as dutiya “second” and tatiya “third” decline like adjectives. Their neuter accusative singular serves as an adverb: dutiyaṃ pi, “for the second time too”.
